config.title: Modules — ESM & CommonJS

intro.title: Modules — ESM & CommonJS
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple application that uses both ES Modules (ESM) and CommonJS to organize and share code between files. You will learn how modules help you split your code into reusable, maintainable pieces by exporting and importing functions, variables, or objects. The core concepts involve using `export` and `import` statements for ESM, and `module.exports` and `require()` for CommonJS. You'll practice by creating separate module files and using them in a main file, seeing how JavaScript handles different module systems. This hands-on approach will give you a clear understanding of modular programming in JavaScript.
intro.usecase: Modules are fundamental to organizing code in modern web applications. When building a dashboard with multiple interactive components like charts, data tables, and user profile panels, each component is typically implemented as a separate module. This allows developers to import only the necessary functionality, making the codebase more maintainable and enabling features like lazy loading. For example, an e-commerce site might use ESM modules for its product filtering UI while using CommonJS modules for server-side rendering logic in Node.js.

objectives: Implement ES Module syntax to export functions and variables
Apply CommonJS syntax to require modules in Node.js
Construct a module that exports multiple values using both ESM and CommonJS patterns
Configure a package.json file to enable ES Module support
Integrate third-party modules by importing them into your application
Manipulate module exports to create named and default exports
Initialize a module system in a JavaScript project with proper file organization

steps.title: Import the CommonJS module using require()

steps.title: Create an ES Module with named exports
steps.instruction: Create a new file named stringUtils.js and define a function named capitalize that takes a string parameter and returns the string with the first letter capitalized. Export it using the ES Module export keyword.
steps.hint: In a new file, write a function that returns the input string with its first character converted to uppercase. Use the export keyword before the function declaration to make it available for import.

// Create your capitalize function here

// Export it using export keyword
steps.expectedOutcome: A new file stringUtils.js is created with a capitalize function that is exported as a named export.
successCriteria: The stringUtils.js file contains a function named capitalize that accepts a string and returns it capitalized, and the function is exported using the export keyword.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created the function, but make sure to export it using the export keyword so it can be imported elsewhere.

steps.title: Import ES Module using import statement
steps.instruction: Import the capitalize and reverse functions from the ES module stringUtils.js using the import statement with named imports.
steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by the named imports in curly braces, then the from keyword and the module path.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing named exports from an ES module
import { add, subtract } from './mathUtils.js';
steps.expectedOutcome: The capitalize and reverse functions are imported from the ES module stringUtils.js using the import statement.
successCriteria: The import statement imports both capitalize and reverse functions from stringUtils.js using named imports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to import both capitalize and reverse functions from stringUtils.js.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax for importing named exports from an ES module. Use import { capitalize, reverse } from 'stringUtils.js';

steps.expectedOutcome: The console will display the capitalized and reversed versions of the sample strings.
successCriteria: The capitalize and reverse functions are called with sample strings and their results are logged to the console.

steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling both capitalize and reverse functions with sample strings and logging the results.
